extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in literature, publishing, and plagiarism controversies
extracted.subtask_short: Wikipedia article on a plagiarized novel
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic article describing the publication, plagiarism allegations, evidence (side-by-side passages), reactions, and fallout surrounding the 2006 young-adult novel How Opal Mehta Got Kissed, Got Wild, and Got a Life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism — identical language and/or common scene or dialogue structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that the book contained numerous passages that 'contain identical language and/or common scene or dialogue structure' amounting to 'literary identity theft.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crown Publishing Group documented 'more than forty passages' with identical language/structure; McCafferty's agent identified 45 'strikingly similar' passages. The article gives multiple side-by-side sample passages as concrete examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent and character of similarities as evidence of intent
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope (number of passages) and character (identical phrasing, shared plot developments, character establishment) of overlaps are used to judge whether copying was accidental or deliberate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and agents argued that the breadth and nature of similarities made 'unconscious' copying implausible; defenders cited youthful internalization or shared tropes. Counts (dozens of passages) and qualitative similarity (plot/character elements) are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's claim of unconscious/internalized similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The author maintained similarities were 'completely unintentional and unconscious' and that she had 'internalized' language from books she read repeatedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a defensive explanation—e.g., Viswanathan said she has a 'photographic memory' and 'never take[s] notes.' The article contrasts this defense with the documented extent of overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passage-by-passage comparison as method for detecting plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Side-by-side comparisons of specific passages from Opal Mehta and earlier works (McCafferty, Rushdie, Cabot, Kinsella, Hidier, etc.) are used as primary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Harvard Crimson and others produced tables/lists of similar passages; the article reproduces several paired examples illustrating near-verbatim or strongly parallel phrasing, scene structure, and imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing plagiarism from shared genre tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative explanation is that similarities reflect widely-used 'tropes' in the chick-lit/YA genre rather than direct copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Harvard Crimson noted it is not always clear whether similarities are plagiarism or common genre conventions; this argument is invoked to contextualize some overlaps and as a partial defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher responses and remediation actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions a publisher may take upon discovery of plagiarism: recall/destroy copies, cancel future contracts, halt adaptations, and decide whether to publish a revised edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Little, Brown recalled and destroyed all shelf copies, canceled the author's second-book contract, and later stated they would not publish a revised edition. DreamWorks halted film development; first-edition copies became collectibles on resale sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public apology, acknowledgment, and proposed revision as mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The author issued a public apology, proposed to add an acknowledgment to the plagiarized author in future printings, and initially proposed revising the novel to 'eliminate any inappropriate similarities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records Viswanathan's statement of remorse and intent to revise; the publisher ultimately decided not to proceed with a revised edition or future publication under contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and potential culpability of book packagers / ghostwriters
rubrics_metrics.description: Book packagers (e.g., Alloy/17th Street) who 'conceptualize and plot' books, sometimes share copyright and may employ ghostwriters; their involvement raises questions of responsibility for copied material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alloy was credited with conceptualizing the book and shares copyright; commentators and affected authors asked whether packagers or ghostwriters might have written/introduced copied passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural-detail appropriation and specificity as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriation of specific cultural or autobiographical details (food, family routines, memories of India) from another author's work is highlighted as particularly indicative of copying rather than generic similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tanuja Desai Hidier documented many specific cultural details from Born Confused that appear in Opal Mehta (e.g., salwar kameez description, detailed food imagery), arguing these are unlikely to be generic tropes and bolster claims of lifting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple independent-source corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of copying are strengthened when multiple different authors identify similar passages in the contested book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article catalogs allegations from several authors (Megan McCafferty, Salman Rushdie, Meg Cabot, Sophie Kinsella, Tanuja Desai Hidier), illustrating how independent identifications across works increase the weight of the accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differing institutional consequences (publisher vs academic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing/industry consequences (recall, contract cancellation, halted film) can be severe, while academic institutions may treat the matter differently (e.g., investigation but no effect on academic standing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harvard investigated but soon stated the controversy would not affect the student's academic standing; by contrast, publisher actions were decisive and public-facing.
